source_text: Ὤιμην γὰρ ἅπαντας τότε τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπους ἠξιῶσθαι· καὶ εἴ τέ τις σοφὸς, δικαιοσύνης μὲν ἐπεμελήθη, ἀδικίαν δὲ ἐξετράπη, καὶ ἔχθραν ἔφυγε πρὸς ἅπαντας δεξιὸς ὢν, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀρεστὸν Θεῷ, οὗτος ματαιοπονεῖν ἐφαίνετο. Τέλος δὲ ἓν ἐδόκει δικαίου τε καὶ ἀσεβοῦς, ἀγαθοῦ τε καὶ κακοῦ, καθαροῦ τε καὶ ἀκαθάρτου, καὶ Θεὸν ἱλασκομένου καὶ μή. Ὅτε γὰρ ἄδικος καὶ ὁ ἀγαθὸς, ὅτε ἐπίορκος, καὶ ὁ τέλεον ὅρκον ἐκτρεπόμενος, εἰς ταὐτὸ τέλος ἐλαύνειν ἠλπίζετο, κατάγνωσίς τέ τις ὕπεισι τοῦ εἰς ὅμοια τελευτᾷν ἅπαντας. Γινώσκω δὲ νῦν ὡς ἀφρόνων ταῦτα ἐνθυμήματα, καὶ πλάναι καὶ ἐξαπάται. Καὶ πολλὰ λέγουσιν, ὡς ὁ ἀποθανὼν οἴχεται τέλεον· καὶ προτιμητέον τὸν ζῶντα τοῦ τεθνηκότος, κἂν ἐν σκότῳ κείμενος ᾖ, κἂν κυνὸς τρόπον, τὸν βίον διαπορεύηται, παρὰ τὸν λέοντα τὸν τεθνηκότα. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ζῶντες τοῦτο γοῦν ἐπίστανται, ὅτι τεθνήξονται· οἱ δὲ νεκροὶ οὐδ᾽ ὁτιοῦν γινώσκουσιν. Ἀμοιβαὶ δὲ οὐδενὸς πρόκεινται μετὰ τὸ ἀποπληρῶσαι τὸ χρεών. Ἥ τε ἔχθρα καὶ ἡ φιλία ἡ πρὸς τοὺς τεθνηκότας, τέλος ἔχει. Ἐκείνων γὰρ, εἴτε ζῆλος, ἐξέλιπεν· εἴτε βίος, ἠφάνισται. Μέτεστι δὲ οὐδενὸς τῷ ἅπαξ ἐντεῦθεν ἀπελθόντι.
thought_title: The false belief that one end awaits all
orientation: Solomon rejects, as the reasoning of fools, his former belief that the righteous and the wicked meet the same end.
pass_a_gloss: For I then supposed all men to have been deemed worthy of the same things; and if anyone wise cared for righteousness, turned from injustice, and fled enmity, being kindly/dexterous toward all, which is pleasing to God, this man appeared to labor in vain. One end seemed [to be] of the just and the ungodly, of good and bad, of clean and unclean, and of the one propitiating God and not. For when the unjust and the good man, when the perjurer and the one wholly turning from an oath, were expected to drive to the same end, a certain condemnation creeps in, of all ending in like things. But I know now that these are reasonings of fools, and errors and deceptions. And they say many things: that the one who died is gone completely; and the living is to be preferred to the dead, even if lying in darkness, even if he passes through life in the manner of a dog, over the dead lion. For the living know this at least, that they will die; but the dead know nothing whatever. Recompenses of nothing lie ahead after fulfilling the fated thing. Both the enmity and the friendship toward the dead have an end. For of them, whether zeal, it has failed; whether life, it has vanished. There is share of nothing for one once departed from here.

pass_b_english: For at that time I thought that all people were counted worthy of the same things; and if any wise man cared for righteousness, turned away from injustice, and avoided enmity by dealing graciously with everyone, which is pleasing to God, he seemed to labor in vain (Ecclesiastes 9:1). One end seemed to belong to the righteous and the ungodly, the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean, the one who seeks God's favor and the one who does not (Ecclesiastes 9:2). For when the unjust man and the good, the perjurer and the one who shuns every oath, were expected to be driven toward the same end, a kind of condemning verdict crept in: that all come to a like end (Ecclesiastes 9:3).

But now I know that these are the reasonings of fools, errors and deceptions. They say many things: that the one who has died is wholly gone, and that the living man is to be preferred to the dead, even if he lies in darkness, even if he goes through life like a dog, over the lion that is dead (Ecclesiastes 9:4). "For the living at least know this, that they will die; but the dead know nothing at all (Ecclesiastes 9:5). No recompense for anything lies ahead once a man has met his fated end. Both the hatred and the love felt toward the dead come to an end. For whatever zeal they had has failed; whatever life they had has vanished. One who has once departed from here has a share in nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:6)."
notes: Numbering is the same in English and LXX. Voice: the first paragraph reports Solomon's former opinion; from 'But now I know' he calls it the thinking of fools, and what follows gives what such people say, not Gregory's teaching (source row note). The Greek moves from indirect statement (ὡς ... οἴχεται ... προτιμητέον) to plain statements; the English marks the fools' words from 'For the living' to the end with quotation marks rather than adding 'they say'. 'The one who seeks God's favor' renders Θεὸν ἱλασκομένου ('propitiating God'), where LXX 9:2 has 'the one who sacrifices'. 'A kind of condemning verdict' renders κατάγνωσίς τις ('a certain condemnation, low judgment'). 'Once a man has met his fated end' renders μετὰ τὸ ἀποπληρῶσαι τὸ χρεών ('after fulfilling what is fated', that is, dying). 'Dealing graciously' renders δεξιὸς ὤν ('being dexterous, kindly'). Ὤιμην is read as ᾤμην. 'Recompense' renders ἀμοιβαί, which covers reward and penalty alike (the 1622 Latin: 'Praemia porro poenasque nullas').
